title: ABM metrics for marketing, sales, and finance
summary: ABM success metrics by owner: the scorecard marketing, sales, and finance each need, the number each one steers by, and the points where numbers change hands.
body_markdown:
**ABM success looks different depending on who's asking.** Marketing wants to know whether the program is reaching the buying committee. Sales wants to know whether it produces meetings worth taking. Finance wants to know what the spend turned into. One dashboard that tries to answer all three at once ends up answering none of them, because the numbers move on different clocks and point at different levers.


So the ABM success metrics worth tracking come in three short scorecards, one per owner, each with a single number to steer by and a clear point where it hands off to the next. We've already written up[the 12 ABM metrics that matter (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/abm-metrics) and[the KPIs for each buying stage (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/abm-kpis) . This post is about who owns which of them.


#### TL;DR


-


Marketing steers by named contacts engaged per target account. Its scorecard covers reach, response, and cost.


-


Sales steers by meetings per target account. Its scorecard covers handoff speed and what happened after the handoff.


-


Finance steers by pipeline-to-spend. Its scorecard covers influenced pipeline with names attached and the ABM cohort against a control.


-


Three hand-off points connect them: a named person engages, an opportunity opens, a budget decision gets made.


-


All three scorecards have to read from the same record, or the first disagreement between them is the last time anyone trusts the report.


## Why one dashboard serves three owners badly


A program-level ABM dashboard usually shows engaged accounts, influenced pipeline, and a conversion rate between them. It looks complete and it answers nobody's question. Marketing can't tell from it whether the ads reached the committee or just the company. Sales can't tell which accounts to work this week. Finance can't open any number and find a deal behind it.


The cause is that each owner's lever moves at a different speed. Named-contact engagement changes in days. Meetings change in weeks. Pipeline arrives a quarter or more after the touches that created it. Blend them and the fast numbers read as noise while the slow ones read as flat. Split them by owner and each person gets a number that moves when they act.


## Marketing's scorecard: are we reaching the right people?


Marketing owns the top of the program: choosing accounts, finding the people inside them, and getting in front of them. Its success metrics are about reach and response, and they should all resolve to identified people rather than logos.


-


**Named contacts engaged per target account.** The steering number. Identified people who visited, clicked, replied, or attended, counted as different people rather than sessions. One is a lead. Three or four at the same account in the same fortnight is a committee forming.


-


**Buying-committee coverage.** Of the roles that have to approve the purchase, how many have you reached? Enterprise committees often run six or more people, so one engaged champion is a start rather than coverage.[What a buying group is (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/what-is-a-buying-group) covers the roles to map.


-


**Cost per engaged contact.** Program spend divided by identified contacts who engaged. It replaces cost per lead, which only counts the small share of buyers who filled out a form.


-


**Signal-to-touch time.** Hours between a buying signal and the first ad or outreach that follows. Interest fades in days, so this is the number that tells marketing whether its own plumbing is fast enough.


What marketing should not carry on this scorecard is anything it can't act on: influenced pipeline, win rate, or the deal count. Those arrive too late to steer by and they belong to the owners below. Marketing's job on the scorecard ends when a named person at a target account has responded.


## Sales' scorecard: are the handoffs turning into conversations?


Sales owns what happens after a person raises a hand. Its metrics are about speed and conversion at the handoff, and they're the ones sales already believes, which is the point.


-


**Meetings per target account.** The steering number, and the one[our ABM playbook (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/guides-and-reports/abm-playbook-step-by-step) is built around. Meetings show up in weeks, sales treats them as real, and deals don't get created without them.


-


**Handoffs acted on.** Of the accounts marketing flagged last week, how many did a rep touch within a few days? If this number is low, the problem isn't the signal.


-


**Pipeline leakage.** Accounts where the buying signals arrived and no sales activity followed. It's found money, and it only becomes visible when marketing's signals and sales' activity sit in the same record.


-


**Stage progression after the meeting.** Whether the accounts that took a meeting moved forward a buying stage in the following month, or slipped back.


The hardest conversation on this scorecard is handoffs acted on, because it measures sales rather than marketing. It's worth having anyway. A program that produces engagement nobody follows up on will be judged on pipeline it never had the chance to create, and marketing will take the blame for it at renewal.


## Finance's scorecard: what did it turn into?


Finance owns the question that decides next year's budget. Its metrics are about outcomes against spend, and every one of them should open to a name, a date, and a deal.


-


**Pipeline-to-spend.** The steering number. Qualified pipeline from target accounts divided by the full cost of the program, including media, data, content, and the hours marketing and sales put in. The playbook's rule of thumb is 5:1, which at a 20% close rate returns roughly a dollar in bookings per dollar spent in year one.[The ABM ROI math (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/abm-roi) walks through it.


-


**The ABM cohort against a control.** Meetings, pipeline, and win rate for the accounts in the program next to the same figures for similar accounts you left in your normal demand programs. The gap is the program's effect, and it doesn't depend on anyone's attribution model. The playbook's own program reported 60% more meetings in the ABM cohort.


-


**Influenced pipeline, with named touches.** Open and won opportunities where marketing reached members of the committee, with the contacts, programs, and dates attached.


-


**Win rate, touched versus untouched.** Deals where the committee saw your ads or content against similar deals where it didn't.


Report these with the single largest deal in and out, say which period the pipeline came from, and call anything under two quarters old directional. Finance will trust a 5:1 you've qualified over a 50:1 you haven't, and that trust is what protects the budget.


## Where the numbers change hands


The three scorecards connect at three hand-off points, and naming them is what stops the owners from arguing about whose number is right.


1. 1


**A named person engages.** Marketing's engaged-contact count becomes sales' handoff. The record that crosses over should name the person, what they did, and when, so the rep doesn't have to interpret an account score.


2. 2


**An opportunity opens.** Sales' meeting becomes finance's pipeline. The touches that happened before this point stay attached to the deal, so influenced pipeline can be opened later and read.


3. 3


**A budget decision gets made.** Finance's pipeline-to-spend becomes marketing's next account list and media plan. If the ratio is short, the first lever is the audience: most wasted ABM spend reaches people who were never part of the deal.


If you're building the internal case before the first quarter of data exists,[getting executive buy-in on ABM (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/getting-executive-buy-in-on-contact-level-abm) covers how to frame it.


## One record, three views


The scorecards only work if they read from the same data. The moment marketing's "engaged" count and sales' "handoff" list are built from different exports, the two owners will disagree about which accounts are in motion, and the disagreement will be settled by whoever argues better rather than by what happened.


Two rules keep the record honest. Don't add company-level reach and person-level engagement into one total; they're different populations and the sum describes nothing. And don't rewrite history when a champion changes jobs; their engagement stays credited to the account where it happened, so the quarterly story holds up months later.

## Frequently asked questions


### What are ABM success metrics?


They are the measures each owner of an ABM program uses to judge whether it is working. Marketing tracks reach and response among named contacts, sales tracks meetings and handoff follow-through, and finance tracks pipeline against spend and the lift of reached accounts over a control group.


### What is the best metric for marketing in ABM?


Named contacts engaged per target account. It moves within days, it resolves to identified people rather than logos, and it is the number marketing can change directly by fixing the audience or the creative.


### What ABM metric does sales care about?


Meetings booked with named contacts at target accounts. Sales already treats meetings as real, they show up within weeks, and deals do not get created without them.


### How does finance measure ABM?


Pipeline-to-spend for the program, influenced pipeline with the contacts and dates attached, and a comparison of meetings, pipeline, and win rate between accounts the program reached and similar accounts it did not. A 5:1 pipeline-to-spend ratio is a common rule of thumb.


### Should marketing, sales, and finance use the same ABM dashboard?


They should read from the same record but use different views. One blended dashboard hides each owner's lever because the numbers move at different speeds. Three short scorecards built from the same named contacts and deals avoid the disagreement.
